Explanation (Vernon, 2018):
Irregular grains showing no crystal-face
boundaries in an igneous rock. Synonym of anhedral
and xenomorphic. The equivalent term for metamorphic
rocks is xenoblastic

Irregular grains showing no crystal-face
boundaries in an igneous rock. Synonym of anhedral
and xenomorphic. The equivalent term for metamorphic
rocks is xenoblastic
A rock containing amygdules, or the texture of such a rock. Amygdule —  gas voids or bubbles in extrusive rocks, filled with secondary minerals (zeolite, calcite, quartz, chalcedony, etc.)
Fine-grained crystalline aggregates not distinguishable with the unaided eye; may be microcrystalline or cryptocrystalline.
Microstructure of volcanic rocks without phenocrysts.

Fine- and medium-grained saccharoidal ( see also: saccharoidal) allotriomorphic grain structure characteristic of some granite rocks, e.g., aplites, which do not contain dark-colored minerals and micas.

Residual large crystals (porphyroclasts; q.v.) in strongly deformed (generally gneissic or mylonitic) rocks. The augen typically tend to be  enticular or eye shaped, and the finer-grained mylonitic foliation is deflected around them. The augen are commonly of K-feldspar in deformed granites. The singular is auge (German for ‘eye’).

A structure commonly found in series of highly deformed sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, where a layer or bed of rigid (competent) rock lying between more plastic (incompetent) layers has been compressed, stretched, and divided into separate blocks at regular intervals. Tectonic lenses — boudins, resembling sausages in longitudinal section, are elongated parallel to the axes of the folds. Syn. sausage structure.
Microstructure of rocks (cataclasites) formed by brittle deformation involving fracturing of grains and relative movement of fragments

A clastic texture is a physical, granular texture in sedimentary rocks characterized by broken fragments (clasts or grains) of pre-existing rocks and minerals that are packed together and bound by a cementing matrix.

A mineral microstructure consisting of a central core of the original grain surrounded by subgrains of the same composition and then recrystallized new grains. This structure indicates rotational recrystallization
Very fine-grained, crystalline material that is incompletely resolved by the microscope

Microstructures of cumulates, which are mafic-ultramafic rocks with more crystals than could be precipitated from the inferred parent  magma; the accumulation of the crystals can be physical (e.g., by crystal settling or floating) or by crystallization processes (e.g., crystallization of early minerals and removal of the interstitial liquid).

Microstructure in which euhedral crystals of plagioclase are completely enclosed by much larger crystals of pyroxene; typical
of the mafic intrusive igneous rock dolerite.
Even grained
denotes a planar foliation texture, formed principally by welding compaction of pumice and glass shards. Pumice fragmennts become elongate and lenticular in this way are termed "fiamme"
Mineral with crystal faces in an igneous rock. Synonym of idiomorphic and automorphic. The equivalent term for metamorphic rocks is idioblastic.
In mineral formations — the structure of aggregates composed of fine-needle and columnar crystals, e.g., the structure of chrysotile and amphibole asbestos.
A homogeneous, or homeoblastic, structure of metamorphic rocks, which is caused by the development of fibrous minerals during recrystallization. See also: nematoblastic.
Parallel alignment of crystals, microlites  or crystallites, reflecting flow of magma
Penetrative planar structure of metamorphic-deformation origin

Gabbroic texture refers to the characteristic appearance of gabbro, a phaneritic (coarse-grained), mafic, intrusive igneous rock. It is defined by large (1 mm+), interlocking crystals of calcium-rich plagioclase and pyroxene (typically augite), often exhibiting an equigranular or sub-ophitic texture. The texture indicates slow cooling at depth, often resulting in a speckled black/dark-green appearance.
Aggregate of phenocrysts formed either by heterogeneous nucleation or synneusis. A crystal occurring in a  glomeroporphyritic aggregate can be called a  glomerocryst’.

Crudely layered foliation typical of coarse-grained metamorphic rocks and deformed coarse-grained rocks, characterized by folia (rich in minerals such as biotite, sillimanite or hornblende) anastomosing around lenticular pods of granoblastic aggregates (rich in minerals such as quartz, feldspar, cordierite or garnet).
vein clay, friction clay [ore deposits]. A thin layer of soft, earthy, clayey material confined to the edges (salband ) of ore veins and to fracture planes. Syn.: selvage [ore deposits]; pug

sin. "Gradational Sorting" . A distinct vertical change in grain size within a single sedimentary layer, transitioning gradually from coarse grains at the bottom to finer grains at the top (referred to as normal grading).

The finest particles are at the bottom and progressively coarsen upward into gravel or pebbles at the top. This is less common and is usually created by dense mass movements like debris flows or grain-flow mechanisms where smaller particles slip beneath larger ones
Aggregate of xenoblastic, equant, predominantly polygonal grains in metamorphic rocks; common in aggregates of quartz (in quartzite), calcite (in marble) and olivine (in peridotite).

The structure of magmatic rocks characterized by microscopic intergrowths of quartz and alkali feldspar. Syn. micrographic. According to Rosenbusch, the structure of porphyritic magmatic rock in which the inclusions and the main mass intergrow with each other during simultaneous crystallization.
Intergrowth of two minerals, each in optical continuity, resembling some forms of ancient writing; most commonly intergrowths of quartz and alkali feldspar

A type of crystalloblastic structure in metamorphic rocks, in which the main rock-forming minerals are divided into two or more groups according to size. The term was introduced by Becke in 1903. Opposite: homeoblastic.

A type of crystalloblastic structure found in metamorphic rocks, in which the main minerals are approximately the same size. Depending on the habit of the minerals, a distinction is made between granoblastic, lepidoblastic, nematoblastic, or fibroblastic structures. The term was proposed by Becke in 1903. Îðpposite: heteroblastic

The texture of rock formed when magma (lava) erupts or is introduced into water, under ice, or into water-saturated sediment, causing it to rapidly cool into glass, granulation, and fragmentation, forming small angular fragments. The term also refers to vitroclastics tuffs — products of explosive volcanism in shallow water conditions or explosions when magma comes into contact with groundwater.
An old-fashioned, not very useful term for granitic microstructure
Mineral with crystal faces in an igneous rock. Synonym of euhedral and automorphic. The equivalent term for metamorphic rocks is idioblastic
Rotational alignment in magma of elongate euhedral crystals that are not internally deformed or of fragments of phenocrysts that have undergone boudinage
A rock structure with a wide range of grain sizes. The term is mainly used for igneous rocks. Syn: heterogranular

Microstructure of mafic igneous rocks (typically volcanic) in which interstices (q.v.) between feldspar laths are occupied by small, relatively equant grains of pyroxene, olivine or opaque oxide minerals
Microstructure of mafic igneous rocks in which interstices between feldspar laths are occupied by a ‘mesostasis’ (q.v.) of quartz, granophyric intergrowths, glass or deuteric minerals.

A jigsaw-fit texture in volcanic rocks is a breccia pattern where angular fragments (clasts) are shattered in place, allowing them to be visually fitted back together, indicating minimal transport or rotation. This texture forms through auto-brecciation, hydro-volcanic explosions, debris avalanches, or thermal contraction.

A type of deformation band observed in crystals under a microscope and visible to the naked eye in foliated rocks. In these bands, the orientation of the crystal lattice or foliation changes or deviates due to slip or displacement. Fracture bands are caused by shock waves, as well as by normal deformation. Conjugate systems of such bands are typically observed.

The texture of a rock consists of very thin layers of varying composition. A rock, such as shale, that consists of thin layers or can be split into thin layers. In sedimentary rocks, the layers are less than 1 cm thick.

A hollow bubble-like structure consisting of concentric shells formed by a fine-grained aggregate of alkali feldspar, quartz, and other minerals. Lithophytes are found in siliceous volcanic rocks, e.g., rhyolite and obsidian.  Synonym: stone bubble.
Small, irregularly shaped cavities (myaroles) in igneous rocks, especially in granites, inside which small crystals of rock-forming minerals protrude.
Older term for finer-grained recrystallized aggregates surrounding porphyroblasts; equivalent to core-and-mantle structure ; the name implies a fragmental origin, which commonly is not appropriate

This texture is called "molar-tooth" texture, because apparently someone thought it looked like the teeth of elephants. Molar tooth structure is a peculiar, synsedimentary feature found almost exclusively in Precambrian (specifically Mesoproterozoic to early Neoproterozoic, ~2600 to 570 million years ago) carbonate sedimentary rocks. It appears as arrays of calcite-filled, often ptygmatically (tightly) folded, and vertically oriented ribbons or nodules within fine-grained, argillaceous (clay-rich) lime mudstones and dolomites.
Microstructure in which euhedral crystals of plagioclase are enclosed or partly enclosed by much larger crystals of K-feldspar; common in the intrusive igneous rock monzonite.
Thinly foliated and strongly lineated rock, commonly with porphyroclasts formed by intense deformation in elongate, relatively restricted zones
Homeoblastic (homeoblastic) structure of metamorphic rocks, characterized by the development of thin prismatic crystals. See also: fibroblastic

Spherical and irregularly shaped inclusions with lobed projections, composed of fine-grained crystalline material and located in sedimentary rocks. The nodular structure is characteristic of anhydrites and other salts.

Microstructure of a sedimentary rock composed largely or entirely of ooids (ooliths, ‘oolites’). Ooids are spherical or ellipsoidal accretions of chemically precipitated aggregates. Limestones rich in ooids are called oolitic limestones or calcareous oolites. Chlorite may also occur as ooids

Spherical structure in granitoid rocks consisting of elongate to fibrous crystals projecting outwards from a nucleus (commonly a phenocryst or enclave) or arranged tangentially; typically the crystals are in rhythmically repeated compositional layers; also see comb layering to which orbicular structure is closely related. The spherical objects making up orbicular structure are orbs, though they are often referred to as ‘orbicules’, which is an unnecessary word invented by geologists.
The structure of an exceptionally coarse-grained igneous rock, with crystals exceeding 3 cm in diameter.

The separation of some volcanic rocks with the formation of isolated masses ranging in size from a few centimeters to a meter or more (usually 30 to 60 cm), resembling pillows or loaves in shape. The pillows fit tightly together so that the convexity of one conforms to the concavity of another. The small spaces between the pillows are filled with either material of the same composition as the pillows themselves or with fragmentary or slag-like material. The size of the mineral grains inside individual pillows usually decreases toward their edges. It is believed that pillow separation occurs during underwater effusions, which is confirmed by the association of pillow lavas with sedimentary, usually deep-water sedimentary rocks. See also pillow lava.
Microstructure referring to large grains with many inclusions in igneous rocks
Structure of a porphyroblast with many inclusions and of a rock with pokiloblasts

Deformed rock with porphyroclasts.  Porphyroclast : Large clast relative to the grain size of the matrix in a mylonite, being a relic of a formerly large grain, such as a phenocryst or a porphyroblast

The term refers to the structure of recrystallized metamorphic rock with large idioblastic crystals possessing high form energy, e.g., garnet, andalusite, which are embedded in the fine-grained crystalloblastic fabric of the rock.

Ptygmatic fold structure. A layer folded into ptigmatic folds. Ptygmatic folds : Folds with rounded hinges and an amplitude almost equal to the wavelength. They develop in separate layers, usually in metamorphic rocks.
Microstructure of pumice (highly vesicular felsic volcanic glass)
Sediment dominated by pyroclastic fragments (volcanic glass and crystals from explosive eruptions).

A breccia that was formed by a volcanic explosion. Syn: eruption breccia, explosion breccia. Key note: Breccias with fragmental cement, usually altered by hydrothermal solutions, are also often referred to as explosive. The explosive nature of such formations is questionable, and the term hydrothermal breccia is more accurate for them.
Phenocrysts of K-feldspar with rims (mantles) of smaller crystals of plagioclase (typically oligoclase) in some granitic rocks
Elongate aggregates of coarse-grained minerals, typically quartz, in high-grade, granoblastic metamorphic rocks; formed either by intense ductile deformation or crystallization in veins.

A bedding surface characterized by the presence of ripple marks. (b) A term that Hills (1963) preferred to current bedding when used to describe the bedding of rapidly deposited sand with fine ripple marks.

A granular crystalline structure resembling granulated sugar. In particular, an granular structure characteristic of aplites, or a crystalline granular structure characteristic of some sandstones, evaporites, marbles, and dolomites. (b) A white (or nearly white) uniformly grained rock with a sugar-like structure. See also aplitic. Syn.: sucrosic; sugary.
Foliation consisting of elongate minerals (e.g., mica, sillimanite, amphibole), commonly anastomosing around porphyroblasts; characteristic of schists
Any structure in rock caused by fracturing, e.g., crushing, shearing, or cleavage structures.
A genetic term used to describe any sedimentary textures formed as a result of underwater landslides.

Sorting in sedimentary rocks refers to the uniformity of grain sizes within a rock or sediment. Geologists classify it based on how similar the particles are, ranging from very well-sorted (all grains are the exact same size) to poorly sorted (a mix of tiny mud and massive pebbles)
Structure of a rock with spherulites; also refers to an aggregate of radiating fibres, not necessarily spherical.

The structure of volcanic rock composed of needle-like crystals of olivine or pyroxene forming a lattice system. It is formed as a result of rapid cooling of very high-temperature melts. Typical for komatiites. This structure resembles the shape of Australian grass, after which it is named.

An organo-sedimentary structure created as a result of sedimentation and cementation during the growth and life activities of microorganisms, mainly blue-green algae. It has a variety of external forms, ranging from almost horizontal layers to columnar, dome-shaped, and spherical formations.

Microstructure in which microlites of feldspar are strongly aligned and wrap around phenocrysts, which may also be aligned, the alignment being due to flow of relatively viscous magma; typical of the volcanic rock trachyte
Pyroclastic breccia consisting of approximately equal amounts of ash, lapilli, and larger volcanic fragments
Detrital sediments of non-volcanic origin containing heterogeneous ash-sized pyroclastic material, such as fragments of crystals, glass, or rocks.

Sediment or rock deposited or considered to be deposited from a turbidity current (turbidity current). Turbidites are characterized by gradational layering, moderate sorting of material, well-developed primary textures, and a sequence of formation consistent with the Bouma cycle (Bouma cycle). The Bouma Sequence (Idealized):(Bottom): Massive or graded sand/sandstone, often with an erosional base. {b}: Parallel-laminated sand. {c}: Current ripple cross-laminated sand and silt. {d}: Parallel-laminated silt. {e} (Top): Pelagic mud/shale, deposited from suspension after the current stops.
Spherulitic texture of basic volcanic rocks. See: spherulitic
Structure of a rock with vesicles.  Vesicle: Spherical or ellipsoidal cavity (former bubble) caused by formation and expansion of gas, typically in a volcanic rock or shallow intrusion.
Veined textures in altered rocks are formed by hydrothermal fluids precipitating minerals into rock fractures.
Sediment composed of fragments of volcanic origin

Structure: They feature undulating, ripple-like patterns formed by the deposition of silt/sand followed by mud. Composition: Nearly equal proportions of sand and mud are common, with continuous mud drapes over ripples
used when glass shards in a pyroclastic deposit have been sufficiently plastic after settling to sinter together during compaction or flow
see allotriomorphic/xenomorphic
Almost all grains are approximately the same size (e.g., exclusively sand).
A mix of particles that fall relatively close to one another in size, but contain a noticeable amount of finer or coarser materials
Grains exhibit a massive range of sizes, including a chaotic mixture of large clasts floating in a dense, fine-grained matrix of silt and clay.
